claims.text: Premelting and melting in HEA nanoparticles are governed primarily by surface segregation of specific constituent atoms.
Differences in atomic size and mixing enthalpy drive the surface segregation that governs melting behavior.
Surface segregation locally reduces cohesive energy at nanoparticle surfaces.
Reduced surface cohesive energy lowers the melting onset relative to the particle core.
Equiatomic HEA nanoparticles can be prepared with a near-homogeneous atomic distribution.
Rapid quenching suppresses surface segregation in HEA nanoparticles.
Post-synthesis annealing or surfactant-assisted synthesis promotes surface segregation of lower-melting-point elements.
The intervention produces a surface compositional gradient involving selected elements.
Atoms with lower bonding energies preferentially segregate to the nanoparticle surface.
Preferential surface segregation of lower-bonding-energy atoms facilitates localized premelting.
Surface premelting begins earlier in segregated particles than in particles with homogeneous elemental distributions.
Nanoparticles engineered for enhanced surface segregation will have a lower premelting-onset temperature than homogeneous baseline nanoparticles.
Nanoparticles engineered for enhanced surface segregation will exhibit a broader melting range than homogeneous baseline nanoparticles.
The segregation effect on premelting will become more noticeable as the surface-to-volume ratio increases.
Rapidly quenched, near-uniform nanoparticles will have a higher and more abrupt melting onset.
The proposed mechanism should hold for HEA nanoparticles below approximately 50 nm when constituent atomic-size and mixing-enthalpy differences are moderate.
The mechanism may not extrapolate to bulk HEAs or to HEAs with very different constituent atomic characteristics.
The magnitude of the premelting-onset shift depends on the constituent elements and nanoparticle size.
